applied.problem: "A motor's rotor always runs a little slower than the field" fails when a load or a drive slowing it pushes the rotor past the field; and "the rotor is a cage of bars" leaves out the wound rotor shown on screen 5.

Four overclaims: rotor 'always' behind (not when driven past the field); speed change 'needs' a drive (screen 5's wound rotor also does it); overload 'more than anything else' is one record's split; 173% is the theoretical figure and can be more.

'No measured figure exists' for cage bar current is stronger than the research shows (laboratory rotors can be instrumented); the honest point is that the picture shows no measured figure and none can be taken on the job.
'Only a few hertz at full load' is not literally true of the lesson's own two-pole motor, whose rotor current runs at 0.83 Hz, under one hertz.

The insulation test step is unsafe once the drive lesson is learned: test voltage on a drive-fed motor's leads can damage the drive, so disconnect it first. The half-load rule of thumb is an approximation and should say 'about'.
Read alone on a card, 'never reaches synchronous speed' fails when a load or a drive slowing the motor pushes the rotor up to or past the field; it holds under the motor's own power.
The quote's 173% is the theoretical figure for a running motor that loses a line; the same guide says it can be higher, so 'about 173%' alone understates it.

'Still draws most of its rated current' and 'Current is not a measure of load' overstate: true of this small motor at light load, but current does rise with load, and larger motors draw a smaller share unloaded.
